paragraphs.text: DIDYMUS, AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS. No opposition of contraries is an opposition in every respect, because contraries also have some things in common. For example, white is contrary to black, but the contrariety lies only in their differences, while colour and quality are common to both. And in none of these cases does the contrariety come first, since everything else comes after what they share, and in what they share there is no contrariety. There must first be colour and quality in common, so that white and black can exist; in the same way, virtue and vice come after quality and disposition. So if there are two unbegotten principles, and they are contraries, then either their contrariety extends to every respect, or there are some things they share. But nothing admits of contrariety in every respect. So these principles too have things in common: existing, being substances, and anything else found to be common to them. But what makes them

contrary is that one is good and the other evil, and that one is light and the other darkness. Their being substances, however, is conceived before their being good and evil. Their contrariety, then, lies not in what they have in common but in what is proper to each. Yet they claim these principles are unbegotten, and nothing comes before the unbegotten. But something does come before them, namely what I said belongs to them in common. Therefore the principles are not unbegotten. For it is as contraries that these are supposed to be unbegotten, yet what they share comes before them. So the principles are not unbegotten, for nothing comes before the unbegotten. They might say that their contrariety does not concern being unbegotten. But then this too will be found to be common to them. And since evil is evil unbegottenly, and good is good unbegottenly, unbegotten evil will be found to be common to both, and unbegotten good common to both. For if good cannot be found without being unbegotten, and being unbegotten is common, then whatever necessarily follows from being unbegotten is also common. And this is the [?]

But suppose they say that being unbegotten is not common to them, but belongs to one and not to the other. Then either the good or the evil is unbegotten, not both good and evil. And if the good turns out to be unbegotten, the evil is begotten. Moreover, every evil deserves punishment, and nothing that deserves punishment is incorruptible. So no evil is incorruptible, since what is corruptible does not exist incorruptibly. Nothing corruptible is unbegotten; evil is corruptible; so evil is not unbegotten. Nothing is evil by substance, because evil is a quality, and no quality is a substance. Therefore evil is not a substance.
All contraries destroy one another, but unbegotten things are indestructible. So they are not contraries, for contraries are not [?]
Nothing unbegotten is changeable. But the good changes when it is overpowered by evil. Therefore the good is not unbegotten.

The unbegotten neither desires anyone's destruction nor destroys anything. But evil desires destruction. Therefore evil is not unbegotten. The divine Scriptures say that not only wicked human beings but the devil himself is handed over to punishment. Everything handed over to punishment is changeable, and nothing changeable is unbegotten. Therefore nothing evil is unbegotten.

Things that are contrary in every respect have nothing in common. So whatever belongs to one of them must by strict necessity not belong to the other. Now existing and being unbegotten belong to the good, so neither of these belongs to evil. Therefore, not existing, the [?]

Everyone who reasonably desires something has that desire fulfilled, if the desire is reasonable. God desires to destroy vice, so vice is among the things that can be destroyed. Being destructible, it will be wiped out, and what is wiped out is not unbegotten. If evil were unbegotten, being evil would belong to it by nature. But no one sins by acting according to nature. So evil would not sin, and what does not sin is not blameworthy. Yet Satan is blameworthy; therefore he is not unbegotten. The divine Scripture says that people are the sons and offspring of the deeds and pursuits they practise. It calls the wrathful, and those who have other sins, "children of wrath," because for this reason they are subject to the wrath of punishment, as Paul says: "And we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest." Such people can change, so that they are no longer children of wrath by nature. Paul, at any rate, speaking of himself and of those who had likewise become holy, says: "We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind," meaning those who are still living in sin. The added words "by nature" do not mean "according to nature" but "in truth." When he says, "We were by nature children of wrath," he shows that those who sin truly are liable to wrath. And just as a person becomes a child of wrath "by nature" because vice is present in him, so by changing he truly becomes a child of virtue as well. Thus the Saviour said of certain people: "Wisdom is justified by her children," calling the wise children of wisdom. Children owe their existence to the one who bore them, and people who have some quality owe their being such to the quality they have acquired. So it is fitting that those who have a quality should be called its children and sons. Just as the Saviour said that the wise are children of wisdom, so he called others sons of peace when he said to the disciples: "If you enter a city or a house, and a son of peace is there, your peace" (the peace given to the city or house) "will rest upon the son of peace who is in it." Again, the same Saviour says: "The sons of this age are shrewder than the sons of light in their own generation." By "sons of light" he means those enlightened by the knowledge of the truth and by the works of virtue. To them, as having become light

because they are sons of light, he says: "You are the light of the world." But those who have loved the present life and direct everything they do toward it he called sons of this age. And though he said they are shrewder than the sons of light, he did not call them shrewder without qualification, but "in their own generation." In other words, they are shrewder than the sons of light in the affairs that belong to this age. For they are wise in doing evil, but they do not know how to do good. Of Judas, too, it is written that he was a son of perdition. The Lord said of him: "None of my disciples was lost except the son of perdition." He called him a son of perdition because he had done the works of perdition. He was not such when he was one of the apostles and served the Saviour together with them, but when he became the betrayer of the Son of God, his Teacher, out of love for the silver of perdition. And that he was not evil by nature is clear, for together with all the disciples he heard: "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves." If the Lord calls sinners wolves and those who practise virtue sheep, then had Judas been evil by nature he would not have been one of Christ's sheep, since one who is evil by nature does not practise virtue. But not even the devil himself is evil by nature; he became so by a turning of his own free will. People are called sons and children not only of base pursuits and deeds but also of good ones, when they carry them out, in the sense explained above: those who receive their being from qualities were said to be offspring of those qualities, because they are what they are from the quality. In the same way it is fitting that someone is called "flesh of sin" and "body of sin," not without qualification, but because he serves sin. For a person who abuses his body and flesh for lust and other such activities makes his body a body of sin and his flesh a flesh of sin, just as a good person sanctifies his own body and soul through chastity and the virtue that goes with it. A virgin, at any rate, becomes holy in body and spirit, that is, in soul, as Paul writes when he says that a virgin should be free from the distractions of worldly affairs, "so that she may be holy in body and spirit." And in the Epistle to the Corinthians he writes: "Glorify God in your body." If God is glorified in human bodies, and God is not glorified in what is evil, then the body is not evil by nature, even if the sinner makes it evil by using it sinfully. And shortly afterwards he again addresses the same people: "Or do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?" "If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him; for God's temple is holy, and that is what you are."

[?] the Apostle writes: "May the God of peace sanctify you wholly, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." How could anyone be wholly sanctified and keep his body whole, if the body were evil and by nature incapable of being sanctified? If it were evil by nature, it could not receive sanctification. But if it receives the good, it is clearly not evil by nature, since it is capable of receiving good. For what is evil by nature cannot receive good, just as what is good by nature cannot receive evil. In another Epistle the same Apostle writes to certain people: "Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God." By these words too he shows that the flesh is by nature capable of being cleansed of the defilements that sin attaches to it, and the same is true of the spirit and soul. If the flesh were evil in substance and the spirit good in substance, the spirit would never have been defiled, nor could the flesh be cleansed of defilement. Yet he commands that both be cleansed of defilement, and he also states the means of cleansing: "perfecting," he says, "holiness in the fear of God." He did well to say "in the fear of God," showing that their obedience comes from themselves and not from compulsion. If, by perfecting holiness in the fear of God, we cleanse our flesh and spirit of defilement, then clearly this happens when holiness comes to dwell in us. For just as the soul is cleansed of ignorance and wrongdoing by the presence of knowledge and justice (since escaping vice brings virtue in, its contrary), so by the presence of sanctification the flesh and the spirit are cleansed of defilement. By "spirit" in these words he means the soul, as in the Acts of the Apostles, when Stephen the apostle was being stoned and was about to die, he said in prayer: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." There, by "his spirit" he meant nothing other than his soul. So in many places the flesh and the spirit are said to belong sometimes to sin and sometimes to sanctification, and to be capable of glorifying God. If so, neither of them is good or evil by nature. Each can receive either by free will. Or does it not, depending on how its possessor uses it, receive each in turn, belonging now to sin and now to sanctification? And if they hold this view because they do not understand the passage they cite to show that the flesh belongs to sin, we will quote it in full and make its meaning plain. It reads:
"God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh." What he means is this.

The flesh of all human beings owes its existence to the union of a man and a woman, except for that of the first-formed man and that which the Saviour assumed. A human body could not come into being in any other way without the male being joined to the female. Since, then, the Saviour took a body from the Virgin alone, a body that did not originate in intercourse, the Apostle called the Lord's flesh a likeness of the flesh that comes from intercourse. He did not simply say that he had the likeness of flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh. And the likeness of sinful flesh is real flesh, differing from all other flesh in this alone, that it came into existence without a man. He who came for the salvation of humankind had to take a body that did not come from such a union. Yet neither could it come from outside the human line of descent, like the first man's, or his body might have been thought to be of a different kind. For had he too been formed from the earth, as the founder of the human race, those who bring in the idea that he only appeared to be human would have had reason to suspect that perhaps he did not truly bear a human body.

Again, if he had taken a body from such a union, with nothing to set it apart, he too would have been thought liable to the sin to which all Adam's descendants were subject. But suppose they say: "If the flesh born from the intercourse of man and woman is sinful flesh, then marriage is evil." Let them hear this. Before the coming of the Saviour, who took away the sin of the world, all people practised marriage sinfully, just as they did everything else with vice. That is how we should understand the bodies born of marriage. And so, since Adam and Eve came together after the sin, their flesh is called the flesh of sin. Adam was incorruptible before the transgression, but he became corruptible by transgressing, and so his descendants inherit corruptibility. The Saviour, then, had the likeness of this flesh, even though his flesh did not see corruption. But when the Saviour came, there was a cleansing [?] from sin in marriage, just as in other matters. Now, at any rate, those who live according to the Gospel can have an honourable marriage and an undefiled bed, as Paul writes to the faithful: "Marriage is honourable and the bed undefiled; but God will judge fornicators and adulterers." In distinguishing honourable marriage, and those who practise it, from fornicators and adulterers, he means that it is neither fornication nor adultery. So marriage is not sin either. It may also be put another way, more in accordance with the nature of things. Virginity is something divine and ranks among the virtues. If, then, someone compares marriage with it and calls marriage sin, marriage is still not sin in an absolute sense. For evil is not evil by comparison with the good;

it is evil by being such in itself. So if something is ever called evil in relation to a good, it may itself be good, only inferior to the good that is preferred to it. Those, then, who come to the Gospel come to it first and foremost in order to worship God and to become wise in God's way. It follows that they will be attacked by certain enemies, for they must take hold of Christianity firmly, and firmness comes from being trained by temptations. They must therefore endure contests. Those who preside over games, if they care about fairness, do not match one athlete against another at random, but take great care to weigh the strength of each. In the same way, Christ, who presides over our contest, does not pair everyone with the same opponents, but assigns each an adversary suited to his maturity and strength. Thus Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were still infants and in the grip of the passions of the flesh: "No temptation has seized you except what is human." Their temptations and contests concerned human affairs. But writing of himself and of those like him, his equals in weight and strength, he says: "Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, and the powers, and the world-rulers of the darkness of this age." He is all but saying: "For us who have risen higher, the wrestling is no longer against blood and flesh, that is, against human things, but against the higher ranks of adversaries." These are kinds of rational beings who have become wicked by their own choice. Let no one suppose that, by speaking of kinds of wicked rational beings, we are speaking of a wicked substance. For there are kinds and classes even of things that exist by choice. We say, for example, that the kinds of good person are the just, the temperate and the prudent. Since virtue is a genus divided into species, namely justice, temperance and the rest, the one who shares in the genus and is therefore good must be, as it were, the genus of those who share in the particular virtues. Likewise, since knowledge is the genus of grammar, music and the rest, we say that the one named "knowledgeable" after the genus is the genus of those named after the particular branches of knowledge. So even if we speak of kinds of wicked rational beings, we mean that all who fall under these kinds are such by choice. Indeed, the wicked names mentioned above signify not substances but choices. The name "devil" signifies not a substance but a choice. Thus Judas too, a man

[?] of this. We call people "devils," that is, slanderers, when they accuse some people to others and those others to them. Since, then, the devil slanders God to human beings, human beings to God, and human beings to one another, he received this name. And if the name "Satan" is also applied to the devil himself, let them know that this too signifies something chosen. It is a Hebrew word, and in Greek it means nothing other than "the adversary." When used of a human being, "adversary" is the same as "enemy" or "one who does harm." Just as an enemy is such by choice, so is an adversary. The same is true of their opposites: "friend," "well-wisher" and [?] "like-minded" are names that signify choices. For a person is called friend and well-wisher in the same way that one is called devil, Satan and evil one. So in the Gospel the Saviour, among other things, teaches the disciples to say this in prayer: "And do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." The name "evil one" too signifies a choice.

If, then, by every name that signifies him, the originator of evil and first deserter from virtue is such by choice, he cannot be evil by substance. They might say that he was evil by substance and also had the chosen traits for which he is so named. But let them know that choice plays no part in what is substantial. No one says that something is a living being or a stone by choice, for these are matters of substance. So nothing about them is a matter of choice, for matters of choice exist only where choice also exists. But perhaps they will say: "Why did the good God bring into being one who was going to be so harmful, a destroyer?" Let those who say this know that they are attacking not only us but everyone who affirms providence. For many others who affirm providence also say that all rational living beings, in whom vice arises, come from God. If, then, they say this about the devil,

they are forced to say it about all rational beings too. We, however, do not follow them. We say that the one who made a being capable of falling into vice by its own inclination is not the cause of vice. He fashioned a rational living being that he wished to be good by its own choice, with free will able to incline either way. He wished it to be good by choosing the good willingly. For no created being can be good against its will; all who are good are good willingly. A being that was to be good by its own choice, then, needed a capacity matching its aptitude for taking up the good. And it followed that what can receive good can also receive evil. To the rational being so constituted, with a capacity for both virtue and vice, a commandment was given, so that it might have virtue in act and vice only as an aptitude. For the Creator's law urges us on, trains us like an athlete, and works with us toward virtue, turning us away from the nature of vice. So even if there is a capacity for vice in the rational being, it is not base because of that capacity. For both virtue and vice have their capacities and their choices. We choose to have the capacity for virtue so that we may be able to take it up in act; we also choose to have the capacity for vice. For we possess vice only when we have its [?] in act. This view is not ours alone; it belongs to all who have reasoned rightly about rational beings. So even if God made the substance now called the devil, he did not create it a devil. He made it capable of receiving virtue, so that it might have virtue, and capable of receiving vice, so that it might abstain from vice. Virtue cannot coexist with vice, and virtue is dear to God. So when he placed the capacities for both in the rational being, he placed them there so that we might bring the one into act and abstain from the end of the other capacity, which is its act. Every rational being, then, was made to be good and not base. If some rational beings have run the opposite course to the one who made them and cares for them, the blame lies not with the one who made them and gave them the law, but with those who set themselves against the [laws] given them and against those who care for them [?]

We see the same thing constantly happening among ourselves. We educate our children, wishing to bring them up in some branch of knowledge so that they may practise it. Yet they do not always practise it as they were taught, but sometimes do the opposite. Many sons whose fathers trained them as physicians do not practise medicine as they should, giving the sick what causes disease instead of what restores health. And surely neither medicine nor the one who taught it

[?]… is responsible. For he did not teach him to act in this way, since he acts otherwise than he learned to act. Again: we instruct certain people so that they may side with justice and reject injustice. But when some of them approach the laws with ill intent, they do the opposite, and we blame neither the law nor the lawgiver. For if the lawgivers themselves were the cause of the injustice, they would not punish the unjust. Their will includes this too: that the unjust person must be punished. In the same way God punishes Satan and those who transgress the laws God has laid down. For he says to some: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” So those who contradict this should know that what they say contradicts itself. For if the devil were evil by essence and alien to the good God, and able to be his equal in strength, God would not have prepared a punishment for him, nor would he be able to cast him into it. Yet Scripture says that fire has been prepared for the devil. This must also be said: if the good God is unchangeable, as indeed he is, and always has the same power, so that he is not able to do one thing at one time and another thing at another, and if after much harm and destruction he was going to hand Satan over to eternal fire, why did he not do this from the beginning, when Satan came against him and took a part of him? For then he would rather have decreed a harsher punishment against him, as for a greater offense. Now Satan harms human beings; but then, according to them, he harmed [?] the Godhead itself, as indeed they believe. And law and just retribution apply more to those who dare to act against a king than to any of his subjects. If we must think in this way, they will attribute to God either ignorance of how he would punish and stop the evil, or weakness. But neither of these belongs to the God of all [?]. So the enemy did not rise up against God as an unbegotten being. Rather, having been made to be holy, he left his capacity for virtue unfulfilled and brought his aptitude for vice into action. For this reason he must be punished, and rightly so, after a long time [?]. And suppose they also bring forward what John the Baptist said to those who came to baptism hypocritically, which runs as follows: “Snakes, brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Bear fruit, then, worthy of repentance, and do not presume to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham. Already the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree, then, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” Let them hear this: they cannot bring forward texts they do not accept.

For they do not accept John the Baptist, since he is one of the figures of the Old Scripture. Still, even so, this must be said to them: through the whole context he rules out the idea that some are good by nature and others evil by nature. For he says to them: “Bear fruit, then, worthy of repentance.” But repentance and its fruit apply neither to one who is evil by essence nor to one who is good by nature. How would one who is always good need repentance? Or how could one who is evil by nature make use of the good of repentance? For one who is evil by essence cannot turn away from sin, and repentance does not happen for the benefit of the good. Moreover, he says that children will be raised up to Abraham even from the stones he was pointing to. By “stones” he means the senseless, people who still persist in vice. For if these repent and believe God, they will be children of Abraham, who was called a man of God because he believed in God, so that his faith was counted as righteousness. We have also heard them say that the words “Snakes, brood of vipers,” addressed to those descended from Abraham and the other holy men, show that Abraham and his people were vipers. They should know that what they say conflicts with the sequence of the passage. For he rebukes these people as not being Abraham's, but a brood of vipers, who pretend and vainly boast that they belong to Abraham. In another passage the Savior says to them: “Abraham did not do this” (Abraham, whom you falsely claim as your father). “If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. But you are of your father the devil, and you want to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and has not stood in the truth.” And he did well to say “has not stood,” showing that the devil had formerly stood in the truth. He calls the devil their father because they resemble him in their turning and in their character. So he did not call Abraham and the holy ones with him vipers. These people became offspring of vipers through a change, because, as has been said, by their own choice they had followed wicked teachers. So John says to them: “Since you chose to become snakes by changing away from virtue (for they were not such by essence), stop being a brood of vipers, whose character you chose to take on. For you were eager to be wicked children of the wicked and unjust children of the unjust. But since you claim that by coming to baptism you bear a sign of repentance, though you do it in pretense, I say to you: Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” For whoever repents does so in order to sin no more and so escape the wrath that will come

upon sinners. He asks, “Who warned you?” to show that one who genuinely teaches people to withdraw from vice does not have them do it in pretense. “But you are doing this hypocritically when you come to be baptized. So you will not be cleansed. For whoever truly wants to be cleansed turns away from sins and bears the fruit of such repentance, doing the works of the disposition opposed to sin. You have not done this, and you have condemned yourselves by claiming to have Abraham as your father. But thinking that you are Abraham's children will not help you. What helps is to be his children both in faith and in fleeing from idols. So even if you were once children of Abraham, that will not save you. For God can make those who are not now his children into his children.” So it is the one who is Abraham's child in virtue who is saved, not the one who has become his child only according to the flesh. And even if someone is that, let him not think highly of himself, for such a status can be lost. Indeed, those who do not have it will be able to acquire it. For Paul too says to those he had not begotten in the flesh: “For in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.” “But when you hear this, do not be contemptuous, as though the wrath against sinners were delayed [?]. For the wicked person already has punishment present to him through his very sinning, since he deserves to be punished. So you should know that the axe is already near the roots of the trees.” By trees he does not mean visible ones, but people shaped by vice. The root of these trees is the worst disposition, from which comes fruit that is not edible but poisonous. So it [bears] no good fruit [?]. Even if the axe signifies punishment and the bad tree signifies the sinful person, these are not opposing natures. For the punishment is threatened in order to change the trees. Whoever threatens sinners wants to reform them by the threat itself. If, then, by threatening with the axe that will cut down the rotten trees, he persuades them to stop bearing bad fruit and to bear good fruit instead, then neither is the tree evil by nature nor is punishment evil by nature. But perhaps they will say: “If punishment reforms the wicked, it is good. But if punishment is good, and the promise is its opposite, and opposites cannot both be good at once, then the promise is evil. But since the promise is not evil but good, punishment is evil. And if punishment is evil, it is not God but Satan who inflicts it.” Yet Satan does not inflict punishment on his own, for they are wicked as he is, and he too would then have to fall under punishment. So he would have to inflict it on the good. But that is impossible. Therefore it is not the evil one who inflicts it, but God. And everything God inflicts is inflicted for a useful end,

since it either produces good or prevents evil. So God, in inflicting this, prevents evil [?]. He would not undertake to prevent evil if it were not possible for evil to be prevented. And what can be prevented cannot exist by nature or be unbegotten. The ignorant also went wrong here, thinking that punishment is the opposite of the promise. For both are recompense: the one brings a reward to the good, the other exacts punishment from those who have willingly transgressed the divine laws. “Always exercise yourself in the doctrines of Providence and judgment,” says the great and gnostic teacher Didymus, “and try to keep their substance in your memory. For nearly everyone stumbles over these. The doctrines of creation [?] […] you will find in the difference of bodies and throughout the world. Those of Providence you will find in the ways that lead us back from vice and ignorance to virtue or to knowledge.” Through much practice and discipline the violence and savagery of the passions are weakened [?]. From Didymus, from the [?] On the Incorporeal. A teacher's instruction and exhortation benefit his hearers not when the instructor [teaches] by word alone, but when he also acts in a way that matches and [?] what he professes. Again, the genuine teacher must lead a life that matches what he lays down for others, so that his deeds are in harmony with his words. IV. Book to Rufinus: Why infants die, even though they took on bodies because of their sins.
